An ordering of binary numbers in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit.
A circuit that selects one of several inputs to pass to its output, according to select lines.
A circuit that adds two bits and a carry-in, producing a sum bit and a carry-out.
The standard way to represent signed integers in binary: the leftmost bit has negative weight; negate by inverting all bits and adding 1.
Adder logic that computes carries in advance from generate and propagate signals, avoiding a slow ripple of carries.
The part of a processor that performs arithmetic and logic operations on binary numbers.
A logic circuit whose outputs depend on its past inputs as well as its present ones, because it contains memory.
The simplest memory circuit: two cross-coupled gates with Set and Reset inputs that store one bit.
A one-bit memory circuit that captures its input at a clock edge and holds it until the next edge.
A chain of flip-flops that moves its stored bits one position along on every clock tick.
Memory that stores each bit in a small latch (usually six transistors); fast, and needs no refresh while powered.
Memory that stores each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor with one transistor; dense, but must be refreshed every few milliseconds.
A sequential circuit (or model) with a finite set of states, moving between them according to its inputs.
A flip-flop hanging between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time when its input changes too close to the clock edge.
Two or more flip-flops in series that give an asynchronous signal time to settle before it is used, making metastability failures extremely rare.
The voltage across a conductor equals the current through it times its resistance: V = IR.
Two circuit rules: current into a junction equals current out, and voltages around any closed loop sum to zero.
Two resistors in series across a supply; the voltage at their junction is a fixed fraction R₂/(R₁ + R₂) of the supply.
The small average speed of charge carriers along a conductor when a current flows, superimposed on their fast random motion.
A material’s intrinsic resistance to current, ρ; a wire’s resistance is R = ρL/A.
How fast charge carriers drift per unit electric field, μ = v/E; conductivity is σ = nqμ.
The product τ = RC, which sets how quickly a capacitor charges or discharges through a resistor (63% in one τ).
The power a digital circuit uses to charge and discharge its capacitances when switching, P ≈ αCV²f.
A material such as silicon with a small band gap, whose conductivity lies between metals and insulators and can be controlled by doping, heat, light or electric fields.
A range of electron energies with no allowed states in a crystal, between the valence band and the conduction band.
The highest energy band that is (nearly) full of electrons in a semiconductor or insulator.
The band of energies above the band gap, nearly empty in a semiconductor; electrons in it move freely and carry current.
The rule that no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state.
The density of electrons (equal to that of holes) in a pure semiconductor, created by heat lifting electrons across the gap; about 10¹⁰ per cm³ in silicon at room temperature.
Adding small, controlled amounts of impurity atoms to a semiconductor to set its number of free electrons or holes.
A semiconductor doped with donors (such as phosphorus in silicon) so that electrons are the majority carriers; p-type uses acceptors (such as boron) so that holes are.
The energy at which an electron state has a 50% chance of being occupied; in equilibrium it is the same throughout a connected system.
The probability f(E) = 1/(1 + e^((E − E_F)/kT)) that a state at energy E is occupied by an electron.
A two-terminal device that lets current flow easily in one direction and very little in the other.
The boundary between p-type and n-type regions of a semiconductor crystal, the basis of diodes, LEDs, solar cells and bipolar transistors.
The zone around a p–n junction emptied of mobile carriers, leaving fixed charged dopant ions and a strong electric field.
The potential step across a p–n junction in equilibrium, V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D / n_i²), about 0.7–0.9 V in silicon.
Shockley’s law for a junction’s current: I = I_s(e^(qV/nkT) − 1).
A diode designed to break down at a precise reverse voltage, used as a voltage reference.
A p–n junction in a direct-gap semiconductor that emits light when electrons and holes recombine; its colour is set by the band gap.
A p–n junction that converts light into electrical power by separating light-generated electron–hole pairs.
A circuit of diodes that converts alternating current into direct current.
A semiconductor device in which a small voltage or current at one terminal controls a larger current between two others; used to amplify and switch.
A transistor made of three layers (npn or pnp) in which a small base current controls a larger collector current; both electrons and holes take part.
In a bipolar transistor, the ratio β = I_C/I_B of collector current to base current, typically 50–300.
How much a transistor’s output current changes per volt of input, g_m = ∂I/∂V; for a bipolar transistor g_m = I_C/V_T.
The slight rise of a bipolar transistor’s collector current with collector voltage, as the widening depletion region thins the base.
A line on a device’s current–voltage graph showing all the operating points allowed by the external circuit; the device operates where it crosses the device curve.
A family of bipolar logic chips (such as the 7400 series) that were the standard digital building blocks from the 1960s to the 1980s.
A bipolar transistor whose emitter uses a wider-band-gap semiconductor than its base, giving very high speed; used in phones and radars.
Metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor: a gate voltage, acting through a thin insulator, creates or removes a conducting channel between source and drain.
A transistor in which an electric field from a gate electrode controls the conductivity of a channel.
The gate voltage at which a MOSFET’s channel forms (strong inversion), typically 0.2–0.5 V in modern logic.
A thin sheet of minority carriers (electrons in p-type silicon) induced at the surface under a MOSFET gate; it forms the channel.
The gate voltage needed to change a transistor’s off-state current tenfold; at least about 60 mV per decade at room temperature.
The thin insulating layer between a MOSFET’s gate and its channel, originally silicon dioxide.
Complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor logic, which pairs n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs so that almost no current flows when a gate is idle.
How far a logic signal can be disturbed and still be read correctly by the next gate, e.g. NM_L = V_IL − V_OL.
In a CMOS gate, the nMOS transistors that connect the output to ground when the output should be 0; its dual, the pMOS pull-up network, connects it to the supply.
A graph of a logic gate’s output voltage against its input voltage.
A pre-designed, pre-characterised logic gate or flip-flop layout from a library, used by software to assemble large chips.
Non-volatile memory that stores bits as charge trapped on a floating gate, erased in blocks; used in SSDs and phones.
An electrically isolated conductor inside a transistor’s gate oxide whose trapped charge shifts the threshold voltage, storing data without power.
A failure in CMOS chips where parasitic bipolar transistors form a short circuit from supply to ground.
A circuit that detects the small voltage difference produced when a memory cell is read and amplifies it to a full logic level.
A complete electronic circuit, with its transistors and wiring, made on a single piece of semiconductor: a chip.
Patterning a chip by projecting light through a mask onto light-sensitive resist, then developing it into a stencil for etching or doping.
Making transistors by diffusing dopants through windows in a protective oxide on a flat silicon surface, with wiring laid on top (Hoerni, 1959).
Gordon Moore’s observation that the number of transistors per chip doubles at a regular rate, about every two years since 1975.
Shrinking a MOSFET’s dimensions and voltage together so it becomes faster and lower-power at constant power density; it broke down around 2005.
The part of a chip that cannot be powered at full speed at the same time because of power and heat limits.
Lithography using 13.5 nm light produced from tin plasma and focused with mirrors in vacuum.
Growing a single crystal by slowly pulling a seed crystal up from a melt; used for nearly all silicon wafers.
The loss of gate control in very short transistors, including threshold roll-off, drain-induced barrier lowering and a worse subthreshold swing.
In a short transistor, the drain voltage lowers the source barrier, reducing the threshold voltage and raising leakage.
The levelling-off of carrier drift speed (about 10⁷ cm/s in silicon) in strong electric fields.
A gate insulator with a higher dielectric constant than SiO₂ (such as hafnium oxide), giving the same capacitance in a thicker, less leaky layer.
The thickness of SiO₂ that would give the same capacitance as a given gate insulator: EOT = t × 3.9/κ.
A transistor whose channel is a thin vertical fin with the gate wrapped over three sides; used from 22 nm (2011–12) onwards.
A transistor whose gate completely surrounds one or more thin channels (nanosheets or nanowires), giving the best electrostatic control.
Silicon whose crystal lattice is deliberately stretched or compressed to raise carrier mobility.
A computer that keeps its instructions in the same memory as its data, as binary numbers (the von Neumann architecture).
The set of instructions a processor understands and how they are encoded; the interface between software and hardware.
The processor register holding the address of the next instruction to fetch.
Overlapping the stages of successive instructions (fetch, decode, execute…) so that a new instruction can start every cycle.
Guessing the outcome of a conditional jump before it is known so that the pipeline can keep fetching instructions.
Executing instructions as soon as their inputs are ready rather than strictly in program order, while preserving the program’s results.
Reduced instruction set computer: a processor design with simple, uniform instructions that are easy to pipeline, such as ARM and RISC-V.
The growing gap between processor speed and the time needed to fetch data from main memory.
Executing instructions along a predicted path before knowing whether they are needed, discarding the results if the guess was wrong.
The speedup of a fixed task on N processors is at most 1/((1 − p) + p/N), where p is the parallel fraction; it can never exceed 1/(1 − p).
When problem size grows with the machine, the scaled speedup on N processors is about (1 − p) + pN.
Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction applied to many data elements at once.
On Nvidia GPUs, a group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction together.
Single instruction, multiple threads: the GPU execution style in which groups of threads run the same instruction on different data.
The number of arithmetic operations a computation performs per byte of data moved to or from memory.
A performance model: attainable speed = min(peak compute, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity).
A GPU unit that performs a small matrix multiply–accumulate in one operation, usually at reduced precision, to accelerate neural networks.
Google’s family of AI accelerator chips built around large arrays of multipliers.
One of several smaller dies combined in a single package to form a larger processor.
Making optical components such as waveguides, modulators and detectors on silicon with chip-manufacturing methods.
Computing hardware inspired by the brain, in which many simple neurons communicate with sparse spikes and memory sits beside computation.
A two-terminal device whose resistance depends on the history of the current that has passed through it.
A quantum bit: a two-level quantum system that can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 and entangled with other qubits.
Encoding one reliable logical qubit in many noisy physical qubits so that errors can be detected and corrected.
A processor designed for one class of tasks (such as neural networks or video) to gain efficiency at the expense of generality.
Field-programmable gate array: a chip of configurable logic blocks and wiring that can be reprogrammed to implement different circuits.
Finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers by repeatedly replacing the larger by its remainder on division by the smaller.
A body immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
Weights balance on a lever when their distances from the fulcrum are inversely proportional to the weights.
A manuscript whose original text was scraped off so the parchment could be reused, often leaving the older writing faintly recoverable.
The science of fluids at rest and the forces they exert, founded by Archimedes.
Brahmagupta’s composition rule: combining two solutions of x² − Ny² = k to produce a new one, the key to solving Pell’s equation.
Bhāskara II’s cyclic algorithm (12th century) that solves every equation x² − Ny² = 1.
The Sanskrit half-chord of an arc, the ancestor of the sine function.
A number less than zero; Brahmagupta called negative numbers “debts” and positive numbers “fortunes”.
The situation in which two different theories predict exactly the same observations, so evidence cannot choose between them.
The time the Earth takes to rotate once relative to the distant stars, about 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds.
Finding the point on a curved mirror at which light from one given point is reflected to another; posed and solved geometrically by Ibn al-Haytham.
Ibn Sina’s thought experiment of a person suspended without any sensation, meant to show that self-awareness does not depend on the body or the senses.
The Moon’s appearing larger near the horizon than high in the sky, though its image in the eye is the same size; explained by Ibn al-Haytham through perceived distance.
In an experiment or trial, a comparison group that does not receive the treatment, used to separate its effect from other causes.
The law of refraction, sin i = n sin r; first described by Ibn Sahl in 984 and later by Snell and Descartes.
Bacon’s four kinds of habitual error that distort knowledge: idols of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre.
The principle that the laws of motion are the same for all observers moving uniformly relative to one another, so uniform motion cannot be detected from inside; first argued by Galileo.
Finding a cause by rejecting every candidate that is absent where the effect occurs or present where it does not, as in Bacon’s tables.
Francis Bacon’s 1620 book proposing a new method of inductive, experimental science to replace Aristotle’s logic.
The changing illuminated shape of Venus seen in a telescope; Galileo’s observation of a full cycle in 1610 refuted Ptolemy’s arrangement of the planets.
A law in which a quantity, such as gravitational force, falls off as one over the square of the distance.
Newton’s view that space is a fixed, infinite container existing independently of the bodies in it.
Leibniz’s view that space and time are nothing more than relations between bodies and events.
A force, like Newton’s gravity, that acts across empty space without any intervening mechanism.
Newton’s three laws: inertia, force equals mass times acceleration, and action equals reaction.
The discovery that differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
Hume’s term for the regular association of one kind of event with another, which is all experience shows us of causation.
Hume’s division of knowledge into relations of ideas (certain but uninformative) and matters of fact (informative but known only by experience).
Kant’s term for judgements that extend our knowledge yet are known independently of experience, such as (he argued) geometry and the causal principle.
The theory, proposed by Kant (1755) and Laplace (1796), that the Solar System formed from a collapsing, rotating cloud of gas and dust.
Laplace’s rule that after n successes and no failures the probability of another success is (n + 1)/(n + 2).
Goodman’s invented predicate (green if observed before a certain time, blue otherwise) used to pose the new riddle of induction.
Random change in the frequency of gene variants from one generation to the next, strongest in small populations.
The faunal boundary through the Indonesian islands, between Bali and Lombok and Borneo and Sulawesi, separating Asian from Australian animals.
The unification, in the 1920s–40s, of Darwin’s natural selection with Mendelian genetics.
The fraction of the variation in a trait within a population that is due to inherited differences.
R = h²S: the response of a trait to selection equals its heritability times the strength of selection.
Whewell’s term for a theory’s explaining many different kinds of facts it was not designed for, which strongly supports it.
Deliberate breeding by humans of plants or animals with desired traits; Darwin’s model for natural selection.
The spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atomic nuclei as they transform into other nuclei; the term was coined by Marie Curie.
The random jiggling of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with its molecules.
The number of particles in one mole of a substance, about 6.022 × 10²³.
The ratio of an object’s speed to the local speed of sound.
The idea, named by Einstein after Mach, that inertia arises from the influence of all the matter in the universe.
Accepting a hypothesis because it explains the available evidence better than its rivals.
The result of special relativity that events simultaneous for one observer need not be simultaneous for another moving relative to the first.
Poincaré’s view that some basic principles of science, such as the choice of geometry, are conventions chosen for convenience rather than facts forced by experiment.
The equations relating space and time coordinates of observers moving uniformly relative to each other in special relativity.
The 1887 interferometer experiment that found no sign of the Earth’s motion through the supposed luminiferous ether.
A ripple in the curvature of spacetime travelling at the speed of light, predicted by general relativity and detected in 2015.
A way of writing a positive whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers, ignoring order; p(n) counts them.
Inelastic scattering of light in which photons gain or lose energy to molecular vibrations, shifting their colour; discovered by Raman and Krishnan in 1928.
A Raman line at lower photon energy than the incident light; an anti-Stokes line lies at higher energy.
A particle, such as a photon, that obeys Bose–Einstein statistics and can share a quantum state with others of its kind.
A particle, such as an electron, that obeys the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two can share a quantum state.
A state of matter in which many bosons, cooled near absolute zero, occupy the same quantum state; first made in 1995.
The formula for the spectrum of light emitted by a body at a given temperature, derived by Planck (1900) and by Bose from photon counting (1924).
Searle’s 1980 thought experiment: someone following rules to answer questions in Chinese, without understanding it, suggests that symbol manipulation alone is not understanding.
Popper’s term for the credit a theory earns by surviving serious attempts to falsify it, as opposed to being confirmed or proved.
Turing’s 1950 test in which an interrogator tries to tell a machine from a human by text conversation; now called the Turing test.
The distance at which a star would show a parallax of one second of arc: about 3.26 light-years, 206,265 astronomical units or 30.9 trillion km.
The distance light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km, or about 63,000 times the Earth–Sun distance.
The slow apparent movement of a star across the sky over years, caused by its motion relative to the Sun; large proper motion suggests a nearby star.
A telescope whose objective lens is cut in two; sliding the halves makes two images, so that small angles between stars can be measured precisely.
The precise measurement of the positions, distances and motions of stars and other celestial objects.
An astronomical object whose true luminosity is known, so that comparing it with its apparent brightness gives its distance.
A pulsating giant star whose brightness varies with a regular period; longer-period Cepheids are more luminous, which makes them standard candles.
A dense, roughly spherical ball of hundreds of thousands of old stars orbiting the centre of a galaxy.
How bright a star would appear if it were placed at a standard distance of 10 parsecs; a measure of its true luminosity on the magnitude scale.
The stretching of light to longer, redder wavelengths, measured as z = Δλ/λ; for galaxies it shows that they are receding as the universe expands.
The present expansion rate of the universe, H₀: the recession speed of a galaxy per unit distance, about 67–73 km/s per megaparsec.
Faint microwave radiation filling the universe at 2.7 K, released about 380,000 years after the big bang when atoms first formed.
A term Einstein added to general relativity in 1917 that acts as a uniform repulsion; today it is the simplest explanation for dark energy.
The unknown cause of the accelerating expansion of the universe, making up about 68% of its energy content.
The explosion of a white dwarf star in a binary system, with a nearly standard peak brightness that makes it a standard candle across billions of light-years.
Matter that does not emit or absorb light and is detected only by its gravity; it appears to be about five times as abundant as ordinary matter.
A graph of the orbital speed of stars and gas against distance from a galaxy’s centre; flat rotation curves are key evidence for dark matter.
The region from which light has had time to reach us since the big bang: about 46 billion light-years in radius today, because of the expansion.
The bending of light from distant objects by the gravity of mass in front of them, used to map mass, including dark matter.
A film exactly one molecule thick, such as oil spread on water; its thickness gives the length of a molecule.
The charge of a single proton, equal and opposite to that of an electron: exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs since 2019.
A microscope that images surfaces atom by atom by measuring a tiny electric current between a sharp tip and the surface.
The conjecture, stated by Riemann in 1859, that every nontrivial zero of the zeta function has real part ½; it implies that the primes are distributed as regularly as possible.
The function ζ(s) = 1 + 1/2^s + 1/3^s + …, extended to complex s; its zeros control the distribution of prime numbers.
The vertical line of complex numbers with real part ½, on which the Riemann hypothesis says all nontrivial zeros of the zeta function lie.
The theorem, proved in 1896, that the number of primes up to x is approximately x / ln x, or more accurately Li(x).
Software, such as Lean, in which mathematics is written formally so that a small trusted kernel can check every step of a proof.
An axis on which equal distances represent equal ratios (1, 10, 100, …) rather than equal differences; constant percentage growth appears as a straight line.
Tufte’s measure of distortion in a graphic: the size of an effect shown in the chart divided by its size in the data; 1 means honest.
Tufte’s term for decoration in a chart that carries no information, such as 3D effects, heavy gridlines and ornamental pictures.
A chart showing one value per category as a dot on a common scale (Cleveland’s dot chart); because it encodes position, its axis need not start at zero.
A bar chart with categories sorted from largest to smallest and a line showing the cumulative percentage, used to find the few causes behind most problems.
A survey answer scale with ordered options such as strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree and strongly agree.
A bar chart in which subgroups are piled on top of one another, so that the bar’s height is the total; only the bottom segment shares a baseline.
A grid of small charts with the same axes and design, one for each group or time, so that they can be compared at a glance.
A sequence of measurements of the same quantity taken at successive times, such as daily temperatures or monthly sales.
A pattern in a time series that repeats with a fixed period, such as every year, week or day.
A smoothed series in which each value is replaced by the mean of a window of neighbouring values; a trailing window lags behind changes.
A chart in which each series is divided by its value on a base date and multiplied by 100, so that all series show relative change from the same start.
A tiny, word-sized line chart without axes, used inline in text or tables to show the shape of a recent history.
A smooth curve estimating a distribution, made by placing a small bump (kernel) on every observation and adding them up; its bandwidth controls the smoothness.
Having two distinct peaks; a bimodal distribution often means two groups have been mixed together.
A plot that stacks the density curves of several groups with a slight vertical overlap, for compact comparison.
Tukey’s text histogram in which each value is split into a stem (leading digits) and a leaf (last digit), so every value can be read back.
A plot that shows a group’s distribution as a mirrored density curve, often with a box plot or quartile lines inside.
A plot showing every observation as a dot, shifted sideways just enough that no dots overlap.
A plot combining a half-violin density (the cloud), a slim box plot and jittered raw points (the rain).
A step curve showing, for each value x, the proportion of observations less than or equal to x; abbreviated ECDF.
Points in a plot hiding behind other points, so that dense regions and small clusters cannot be seen.
Locally weighted scatter-plot smoothing: a smooth trend line made by fitting weighted straight lines to the neighbourhood of each point.
Counting the points of a scatter plot in a grid of hexagons and colouring each by its count, a two-dimensional histogram for large data.
A scatter plot in which marker size represents a third variable; size should be proportional to area.
A line through a plotted point showing variability or uncertainty, such as ±1 SD, ±1 SE or a 95% confidence interval; the caption must say which.
A chart showing the estimates and confidence intervals of several studies, with a pooled estimate (diamond) from a meta-analysis.
A chart joining each item’s values at two times or conditions with a line, making changes and rank swaps easy to see.
A forecast chart with bands of decreasing shading showing ranges of increasingly unlikely outcomes.
A grid of coloured cells representing a table of numbers, with colour encoding each value.
A colour scale running from light to dark (or the reverse) for quantities that go from low to high.
A colour scale with two contrasting hues meeting at a neutral middle, for data with a meaningful centre such as zero.
A tree diagram showing how items were grouped by hierarchical clustering; branches joining lower down are more similar.
A plot with one vertical axis per variable, in which each data point is a line crossing every axis at its value.
A chart with variables on spokes radiating from a centre, each item drawn as a polygon; also called a spider or star chart.
A plot of the difference between two measurement methods against their average, with the mean bias and 95% limits of agreement.
A plot of study effect estimates against their precision; asymmetry can indicate publication bias.
A plot of the size of change (fold change) against the strength of evidence (−log₁₀ p) for many tests at once.
A rectangle divided into nested smaller rectangles whose areas are proportional to the sizes of the items in a hierarchy.
A hierarchy drawn as concentric rings, each divided into segments whose angles are proportional to size.
A display of a table of counts in which tile areas are proportional to counts; misaligned divisions show association between the variables.
A chart showing how a starting total changes through a series of positive and negative steps to a final total; also called a bridge chart.
A flow diagram in which the width of each band is proportional to the quantity flowing between stages.
A calibration plot comparing predicted probabilities with the observed frequency of the event in bins of predictions.
t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding: a method for mapping high-dimensional data to two dimensions that keeps similar points close together.
Uniform manifold approximation and projection: a fast method for mapping high-dimensional data to two or three dimensions.
A relationship of the form y = a·xᵇ, which appears as a straight line with slope b on log–log axes.
A map of a surface drawn with lines joining points of equal value; closely spaced lines mean steep change.
A plot of how the frequency content of a signal changes over time, with colour showing intensity.
A step-shaped estimate of the proportion of subjects who have not yet had an event over time, which correctly handles censored observations.
In survival analysis, a subject whose event had not happened when follow-up ended, so that only a lower bound on their time is known.
A plot of a process measurement over time with a centre line and control limits, used to tell ordinary variation from special causes.
The power to which a base must be raised to give a number: the base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3, because 10³ = 1000. It turns multiplication into addition.
The logarithm to base e ≈ 2.71828, written ln. Its rate of change is 1/x, and it equals the area under the curve 1/x from 1 to x.
The constant e = 2.71828…, the limit of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n grows, and the base of natural logarithms.
The power of ten nearest to a quantity; two quantities differ by one order of magnitude when one is about ten times the other.
A calculating instrument with logarithmic scales that slide against each other, so that adding lengths multiplies numbers.
The time a quantity growing by a fixed percentage takes to double: ln 2 divided by the continuous growth rate, roughly 70 divided by the percentage rate.
Growth by a fixed percentage in each equal step of time, so that the quantity doubles at regular intervals; a straight line on a logarithmic axis.
A logarithmic unit for a ratio of powers: ten times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio. Each 10 dB is a factor of ten in power.
A graph with logarithmic scales on both axes, on which a power law y = a·xᵇ appears as a straight line of slope b.
The pattern that in many data sets spanning several orders of magnitude, the first digit d occurs with probability log₁₀(1 + 1/d), so about 30% start with 1.
A way of computing log(eᵃ + eᵇ + …) without overflow or underflow, by first subtracting the largest value.

A function beyond powers, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions that arises so often (from integrals, differential equations or series) that it has a standard name, such as the gamma or Bessel function.
Γ(x), the extension of the factorial to non-whole numbers: Γ(n) = (n − 1)! and Γ(x + 1) = x Γ(x).
erf(x), the integral of a Gaussian bell from 0 to x scaled so that erf(∞) = 1; it gives areas under the normal curve and diffusion profiles.
A solution of Bessel’s equation, written Jₙ(x); a slowly decaying wave that describes vibrations and waves in circles and cylinders.
One of a family of orthogonal polynomials Pₗ(x) on the interval from −1 to 1, used to describe how quantities vary with angle around an axis.
Functions on the surface of a sphere, Yₗᵐ(θ, φ), that play the role of a Fourier series there; they give the shapes of atomic orbitals.
A family of polynomials whose products integrate to zero (with some weight) unless they are the same, so they can be combined like Fourier modes.
The wild oscillation near the ends of an interval when a high-degree polynomial is fitted through equally spaced points; Chebyshev points avoid it.
An integral involving the square root of a cubic or quartic polynomial, such as the arc length of an ellipse or the exact period of a pendulum.
A power series ₂F₁(a, b; c; z) with a simple ratio between terms; many special functions are special cases of it.
The function W(z) that solves w eʷ = z, used for equations that mix a variable with its exponential.
